questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
- Tests knowledge of per-namespace tooling with standard CKAD primitives (PVCs, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, Secrets, sidecars, probes, NetworkPolicy).
- Exercises end-to-end flow: manifest reading, batching, external POST, and secure networking.

Key Concepts
- InitContainer installation of scanners
- PVC-mounted manifests and ConfigMap-driven batching
- Secret-based credentials and TLS rotation sidecar
- Readiness/Liveness probes and per-namespace NetworkPolicy
- Minimal YAML skeleton and trade-offs between latency and throughput

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-scan-guardian
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: image-scan-guardian
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-scan-guardian
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: scanner
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 60; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - mountPath: /images
              name: images
        - name: main
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo running; sleep 3600"]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: image-config
      initContainers:
        - name: install-scanner
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache --update curl jq && echo scanner installed"]
      volumes:
        - name: images
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: images-pvc
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: reg secret
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle partial failures in batch processing?
- What RBAC changes are appropriate for this per-namespace task?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Assess ability to constrain scheduling to hardware and perform safe rolling updates for GPU workloads.

## Key Concepts
- NodeSelector and taints/tolerations
- GPU resource requests/limits
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- RollingUpdate strategy and preStop
- Verification and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ai-processor
  namespace: ml
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ai-processor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ai-processor
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        hardware: gpu
      tolerations:
      - key: hardware
        operator: Equal
        value: gpu
        effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
      - name: ai-processor
        image: your-image:tag
        resources:
          requests:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1
            memory: "2Gi"
            cpu: "500m"
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1
            memory: "4Gi"
            cpu: "1000m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /live
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 1
```

## Verification Under Load
1. Deploy and verify pods schedule on GPU nodes: `kubectl get pods -n ml -o wide`
2. Check GPU allocation: `kubectl describe nodes | grep nvidia.com/gpu`
3. Load test with concurrent requests while monitoring pod health
4. Verify rolling updates maintain availability: `kubectl rollout status deployment/ai-processor -n ml`
5. Monitor GPU utilization during load: `nvidia-smi` on target nodes

## Rollback Strategy
1. Use deployment revision history: `kubectl rollout history deployment/ai-processor -n ml`
2. Quick rollback: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/ai-processor -n ml`
3. For critical issues, scale to zero then redeploy previous stable version
4. Monitor rollback progress and verify pod health and GPU allocation

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical lifecycle management and how probes interact with rolling updates to avoid downtime.

## Key Concepts

- StartupProbe, readinessProbe, livenessProbe
- preStop and terminationGracePeriodSeconds
- Graceful shutdown patterns in Node.js apps

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-server
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-server
        image: node:18
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 3000
          failureThreshold: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 15
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["bash","-lc","sleep 5"]
        terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log
        terminationMessagePolicy: File
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adjust thresholds for busy traffic?
- How would you verify graceful shutdown under load?
- What pitfalls exist with preStop sleeps in container runtimes?

## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical CKAD pattern: file-driven config synchronization, idempotent object creation, secret management, and namespace-scoped network policy.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer tooling, kubectl in-cluster, ConfigMap/Secret management, TLS sidecar, NetworkPolicy scoping.
- Cadence-based reconciliation and minimal YAML skeletons for CKAD.

## Code Example
```javascript
# Minimal skeleton for a Deployment that performs config sync
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-sync
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-sync
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache jq curl kubectl"]
      containers:
        - name: main
          image: my-registry/config-sync:latest
          env:
            - name: SYNC_INTERVAL
              value: "300s"
      volumes:
        - name: config
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-pvc
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 10
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 30
        periodSeconds: 10
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you secure the TLS sidecar and rotate certs without restarting pods?
- How would you test reconciliation and conflict resolution between file changes and cluster objects?

## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to choreograph ephemeral canaries using core CKAD primitives: templated Deployment from ConfigMap, secret-based auth, logs via PVC, init containers, probes, and namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- ConfigMap templating for Deployment
- Secret-based API tokens and restricted RBAC
- PVC-backed logs and cleanup discipline
- InitContainers for tooling bootstrap
- Readiness/Liveness probes for short-lived canaries
- NetworkPolicy scoped to external dashboard

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-tester
spec:
  schedule: "*/20 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
          containers:
            - name: canary
              image: my-canary-image:latest
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/canary/run.sh"]
              env:
                - name: DASHBOARD_TOKEN
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: canary-token
                      key: token
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: canary-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you rollback a failing canary and propagate the status to the dashboard?
- What are the memory/CPU considerations for rapid-canary spikes and how would you cap them?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD proficiency across namespace-scoped automation, ConfigMap manipulation, InitContainers, and secure egress controls in real-world migration workflows.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scoped to a namespace with per-namespace behavior
- InitContainer to install tooling (yq) and prepare environment
- ConfigMap-driven migration plan and idempotent updates
- PVC-backed logs and a Secret-backed external POST
- Readiness/Liveness probes for resilient Jobs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to the migration portal

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: per-namespace CronJob migrating ConfigMaps
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: config-migrate
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  schedule: "0 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: migrate-sa
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache go && go install github.com/mikefarah/yq@latest"]
          containers:
          - name: migrate
            image: my-registry/config-migrate:latest
            envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: migration-api
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotent migrations across runs?
- How would you handle partial failures or large numbers of ConfigMaps?
- What monitoring would you add to detect drift or failures?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question validates understanding of per-namespace resource governance in Kubernetes. It tests knowledge of how LimitRange and ResourceQuota work together to control pod sizing and cluster resource allocation.

## Key Concepts
- **LimitRange**: Sets default requests/limits applied to Pods that don't specify resources
- **ResourceQuota**: Enforces hard limits on total namespace resource consumption
- **Policy alignment**: Ensuring Deployments specify resources matching namespace defaults
- **Verification**: Testing policy enforcement with intentional over-allocation
- **Rollback**: Strategy for removing or scaling back resources when policies need adjustment

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: analytics-lr
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: 128Mi
```
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: analytics-quo
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  hard:
    cpu: "400m"
    memory: 512Mi
    requests.storage: "1Gi"
```
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: reporter
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reporter
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
```
## Verification Commands
```bash
kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl apply -f quota.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl describe resourcequota analytics-quo -n analytics
kubectl run overload-test --image=busybox --restart=Never --requests=cpu=500m,memory=600Mi --dry-run=server
```
## Rollback Strategy
```bash
kubectl delete -f quota.yaml
kubectl delete -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl scale deployment reporter --replicas=0 -n analytics
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose common CKAD primitives into a cohesive, maintainable per-namespace app: InitContainer logic, ConfigMap-driven behavior, TLS handling, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer installs rendering tool and pre-processes inputs
- ConfigMap and Secret drive runtime config and secrets
- Sidecar for TLS rotation and secret refresh
- Readiness/Liveness probes for quick failure detection
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to internal endpoints

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: docs-portal
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: docs-portal
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: docs-portal
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: docs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: docs-pvc
        - name: tls-cert
          secret:
            secretName: docs-tls
      initContainers:
        - name: render-md
          image: pandoc/pandoc:latest
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp -r /docs/* /rendered/; pandoc -f markdown -t html /docs/*.md -o /rendered/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: docs
              mountPath: /docs
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /rendered
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:stable
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of combining Kubernetes primitives for a practical, beginner-to-intermediate task: ConfigMaps and Secrets for config and credentials, InitContainers for bootstrapping, a TLS rotation sidecar for security, probes for reliability, and a Namespace NetworkPolicy to constrain egress.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap and Secret usage in a single pod
- InitContainer for bootstrapping dependencies
- Sidecar for TLS cert rotation
- Readiness and Liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to constrain egress

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: proxy
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-deps
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["/bin/sh","-lc","apk add --no-cache python3 py3-pip && pip3 install fastapi uvicorn httpx"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config
      containers:
      - name: proxy
        image: myorg/proxy:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
        - secretRef:
            name: api-credentials
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: app-config
      - name: certs
        secret:
          secretName: tls-certs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test the rate limiter under burst traffic?
- How would you rotate keys without downtime?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD ability to combine common primitives: PVC-backed data, ConfigMap-driven behavior, Secrets for credentials, InitContainers, TLS rotation sidecar, probes, and per-namespace NetworkPolicy in a cohesive, beginner-friendly scenario.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap/Secret usage for runtime config and credentials
- PVC-backed storage and data lifecycle
- InitContainer for dependencies
- TLS cert rotation sidecar
- Readiness/Liveness probes and health checks
- NamespaceNetworkPolicy scoping

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ns-api
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: ns-app-data
      initContainers:
        - name: install-deps
          image: python:3.11
          command: ["bash","-lc","pip install flask sqlite3"]
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myregistry/ns-api:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: ENABLE_FEATURE
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: ENABLE_FEATURE
            - name: API_TIMEOUT
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: API_TIMEOUT
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: quay.io/cert_manager/tls-sidecar:latest
        # sidecar config omitted for brevity
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      restartPolicy: Always
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test config flag changes without rolling pods?
- What are trade-offs of storing DB in a PVC vs ephemeral storage?
